newsitem.title: USA: Transatlantic arb shut for US Gulf Coast refiners.
newsitem.headline: Transatlantic arb shut for US Gulf Coast refiners.

text.p: North Sea crudes evaporated from the Gulf Coast on Thursday, reflecting the closed transatlantic arbitrage, traders said.
"The window is pretty well shut," said one European trader based in the Northeast.
The April spread between West Texas Intermediate/Cushing and Brent was around $1.50 a barrel.
West African crudes remained bountiful, although Gulf Coast demand for these grades was seen as slack.
Nigerian Qua Iboe was assessed at April WTI plus 40 cents a barrel. Bonny Light, Brass River and Forcados were pegged at similar levels.
Traders blamed the flood of West African crudes on sluggish Asian and European demand.
Elsewhere, U.S. overseers approved the 34th contract for Iraq to sell 3.6 million barrels of crude, or 40,000 barrels per day (bpd), to Indian Oil Corp.
The deal puts Iraq at the $1 billion monetary cap for the first 90-day period of the six-month agreement.
Separately, various Iraqi spot cargoes are on offer in the Gulf, but interest is minimal, traders said.

In Latin America, Colombian Cano Limon, which some traders contend has dropped as a result of Exxon's unconfirmed cutoff of spot purchases, was assessed at April WTI minus $2.00 a barrel for loading in early to mid-March.
Some Gulf Coast refiners are still in turnarounds, although the maintenance season is passing its peak, traders said.
